extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming clear, appropriate general conceptions, naming and definitions in the context of inductive inquiry; covers how to observe/compare, select class-defining properties, and fix meanings of general names for scientific use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The clearness of our conceptions chiefly depends on the carefulness and accuracy of our observing and comparing faculties, and on never using general names without a precise connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires habit of minute observation, accurate memory for results, and precise connotation for general names; vague or habitual misclassification indicates lack of clear idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of conceptions to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions are not merely to be clear but must be appropriate for the purpose; the properties included must be those which will help toward what we wish to understand (either deepest nature or the particular property under investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When framing classes choose properties relevant to theoretical or practical aims; a clear conception that omits properties important to the problem is not appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality of classes (classes must correspond to real distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary condition is that the class be really a class; it must correspond to a real distinction — the things it includes must really agree with one another in certain particulars and differ from others in those same particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grouping items that have no common properties or only properties also possessed by other things; classification should reflect genuine sameness/difference in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select class-defining properties that are causally or inferentially central
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting among common properties to fix a name's connotation, choose those on which many others depend, or which are sure marks of them, from which many others will follow by inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer properties that penetrate 'deeply into the nature' of things or are known by experience/deduction to determine other attributes; sometimes the best mark is not the most familiar one (example: definition of life by continuous decomposition/recomposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanently fixed premature conceptions; be willing to revise
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions formed without thorough knowledge are inevitable in progress but become impediments only when permanently acquiesced in; habitually grouping things in wrong classes and refusing to exchange them for better ones causes errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat early conceptions as provisional; update classifications and definitions as knowledge of phenomena and their relevant conditions increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior conceptions and hypotheses when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The really important agreement in phenomena sometimes cannot be discovered by mere comparison; one may need previous conceptions or hypotheses and the scientific imagination to arrange known elements into new, plausible combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stored general conceptions and imaginative hypotheses to guide where to search for hidden agreements; but test these conjectures against facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (general names) as instrument for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: General names and propositions are not strictly necessary for the simplest inductions, but they are indispensable for carrying induction beyond immediate, simple cases — they record uniformities and make complex reasoning and memory practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words and general propositions to register uniformities discovered by experiment/comparison so they can serve as formulas for future inferences; without general names we could not assert propositions about classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every general name must have a certain and knowable meaning (fixed connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every general name should have a meaning steadily fixed and precisely determined; the meaning of a general connotative name resides in the connotation — the attribute(s) it expresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix connotation by specifying the attribute(s) connoted; for existing common names, ascertain and fix the connotation they already bear rather than inventing a wholly new one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define names by analyzing common properties (explication of conceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To give a connotation to a name, especially one in common use, is the logician's task: to analyze the vague feeling of resemblance into particular circumstances of resemblance and ascertain which points produce the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the things feature-by-feature to determine shared attributes; this may require inductive operations to find unobvious agreements that explain obvious likenesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect received usage when fixing meanings of established names
rubrics_metrics.description: In fixing the connotation of a concrete name already in use, avoid meanings that conflict with prior habits and generally received propositions; the fixed connotation should be in agreement (as far as it goes) with the vague connotation already held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions that preserve existing true propositions involving the term; radical redefinitions that contradict entrenched, true uses are undesirable and impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition must serve an enunciable proposition (utility of definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition has scientific value only when associated with some proposition it is to express; the attempt to define is valuable insofar as it enables true propositions and furthers knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before finalizing a definition, ask what principle or proposition it serves; a definition aimed at explaining a conception should be immediately usable in asserting truths or laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are part of discovery and require sagacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of definition is part of the business of discovery; to define usefully requires sagacity by which truth is detected, and presupposes some knowledge of the truth to be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining well presumes substantial understanding of the object's properties and causal relations; one often must know what truth one aims to express before settling the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should be progressive and open to improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to frame a perfect set of definitions until the theory of the subject is perfect; as science advances, definitions should be improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to revise definitions when new knowledge about the objects and relations arises; definitions are not final but evolve with theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vagueness and ambiguous extension of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague connotations allow extension by degrees (A similar to B, B to C, etc.), potentially leading a name to pass to things scarcely resembling the originals; such vagueness prevents precise induction and testable propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to multiple derived senses of a word and to transitive extension across intermediate affinities; where necessary, disambiguate or restrict sense to preserve testability of general propositions.
